SECTION 2: CORE CLINICAL PHILOSOPHY & SURGICAL PATHWAYS
================================================================================

2.1 JOINT PRESERVATION FIRST
Dr. Modi's practice is founded on joint preservation. Native anatomy is conserved whenever biologically and biomechanically feasible:
- In Meniscal Pathology: Prioritize meniscal repair, root repair, and ramp lesion repair over meniscectomy to preserve contact surface area and avert accelerated joint space loss.
- In Cartilage Damage: Deploy biological restoration (microfracture with matrix augmentation, osteochondral autograft transfer - OATS, autologous chondrocyte implantation) before end-stage arthritis develops.
- In Alignment Deformities: Perform corrective osteotomy (High Tibial Osteotomy - HTO, Supracondylar Focal Dome Osteotomy) to offload damaged compartments, delaying or preventing total knee arthroplasty in young active individuals.
- In Rotator Cuff Disease: Attempt structured evidence-based physical therapy and subacromial biomechanical rehabilitation for degenerative partial-thickness tears, reserving surgery for acute traumatic tears or refractory symptomatic full-thickness defects.

2.2 DIAGNOSTIC RIGOR & PHYSICAL EXAMINATION PROTOCOLS
Accurate physical examination is the cornerstone of orthopaedic diagnosis before imaging correlation:
- Knee Assessment:
  * Lachman Test (30° flexion): Most sensitive clinical test for ACL integrity (>95% sensitivity).
  * Pivot-Shift Test: Gold standard for dynamic rotational anterolateral instability.
  * McMurray Test & Thessaly Test (20° dynamic load): Meniscal tear localization with joint line tenderness.
  * Dial Test (30° and 90°): Differentiates isolated posterolateral corner (PLC) injury from combined PCL-PLC instability.
- Shoulder Assessment:
  * Empty Can (Jobe) & Full Can Tests: Supraspinatus tendon integrity.
  * Hornblower's Sign & External Rotation Lag Sign: Infraspinatus and teres minor pathology.
  * Bear-Hug & Belly-Press Tests: Subscapularis tendon tears.
  * O'Brien Active Compression Test & Speed's / Yergason's Tests: Superior labral anterior-posterior (SLAP) and long head of biceps pathology.
  * Apprehension, Relocation, and Surprise (Release) Tests: Anterior glenohumeral instability and Bankart lesions.
- Hip & Groin Assessment:
  * FADIR Test (Flexion-Adduction-Internal Rotation): High sensitivity for anterior Femoroacetabular Impingement (FAI) and acetabular labral tears.
  * FABER Test (Flexion-Abduction-External Rotation / Patrick's): Differentiates sacroiliac pathology and hip capsule tightness.
  * Resisted Straight Leg Raise (Stinchfield Test): Intra-articular hip pathology.
  * Doha Consensus Groin Palpation: Adductor-related, iliopsoas-related, inguinal-related, and pubic-related clinical entities.
- Foot & Ankle Assessment:
  * Thompson Squeeze Test & Matles Sign: Pathognomonic for acute complete Achilles tendon rupture.
  * Ottawa Ankle & Foot Rules: High-sensitivity criteria to eliminate unnecessary radiographs in acute ankle and midfoot trauma.
  * Anterior Drawer & Talar Tilt Tests: Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) and calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) mechanical laxity.
- Elbow & Wrist Assessment:
  * Cozen's & Mill's Tests: Common extensor origin tendinopathy (lateral epicondylalgia / Tennis Elbow).
  * Resisted Wrist Flexion & Pronation: Medial epicondylalgia (Golfer's Elbow).
  * Watson's Scaphoid Shift Test: Scapholunate ligament dissociation.
  * Finkelstein's Test: De Quervain's tenosynovitis of the first dorsal compartment.

2.3 STEP-BY-STEP SURGICAL TECHNIQUE PRINCIPLES
- Arthroscopic ACL Reconstruction:
  * Anatomical graft positioning utilizing independent transportal or outside-in femoral drilling to place the graft in native femoral and tibial footprints.
  * Graft Selection: Hamstring tendon autograft, bone-patellar tendon-bone (BPTB), or quadriceps tendon autograft customized to patient age, hypermobility, sporting demands, and occupational biomechanics.
  * Anterolateral Augmentation (Lateral Extra-Articular Tenodesis - LET): Indicated in revision cases, high-grade pivot shift, hyperlaxity, or elite pivot athletes to protect the intra-articular graft.
- Arthroscopic Rotator Cuff Repair:
  * Double-Row Knotless Suture-Bridge Construct: Maximizes footprint contact area, restores anatomical footprint pressure, and minimizes gap formation under cyclic physiological loading.
  * Subacromial decompression and bursectomy performed selectively to eliminate mechanical impingement without destabilizing the coracoacromial arch.
  * Biceps Management: Suprapectoral or subpectoral tenodesis versus tenotomy for degenerate, subluxating long head of biceps lesions.
- Arthroscopic Shoulder Labrum Repair:
  * Bankart Repair: Mobilization of the anteroinferior labrum and glenoid neck decortication, followed by anatomical re-anchoring using 3 to 4 suture anchors placed at the 3:00, 4:00, and 5:00 glenoid rim positions.
  * SLAP Repair: Suture anchor fixation of the superior labrum-biceps complex for Type II tears in young overhead athletes, or tenodesis in older / non-throwing cohorts.
  * Posterior Labral Repair: Knotless anchor repair for reverse Bankart lesions in contact athletes with posterior instability.
- Meniscal Preservation:
  * All-inside suture repair for posterior horn tears using modern low-profile devices.
  * Inside-out horizontal mattress sutures for midbody and body-junction tears to minimize neurovascular risk and provide maximal compression.
  * Transosseous pullout repair for meniscal root tears to restore circumferential hoop stress transmission and halt rapid joint degeneration.

- Clinical Content Synopsis: An ACL (anterior cruciate ligament) tear is one of the most well-known and feared sports injuries. If you recently injured your knee and wonder whether you may have torn your ACL, or if you have just been diagnosed and want to understand what lies ahead, this guide is for you. We will cover what the ACL is, how it gets injured, what it feels like, how it is diagnosed, and your treatment options. --- ## What Is the ACL? The anterior cruciate ligament is a strong band of fibrous tissue inside your knee that connects the thigh bone (femur) to the shin bone (tibia). Along with three other ligaments, it keeps the knee stable during movement, particularly the rotational and forwards-backwards forces involved in cutting, pivoting, and landing. [1] The ACL is one of the knee's most critical stabilisers. When it tears, the knee often loses its ability to function reliably under the demands of sport or vigorous physical activity. --- ## How Does an ACL Tear Happen? ACL injuries most commonly occur without any direct contact to the knee. The typical mechanisms include: - **Sudden change of direction or cutting movements**: planting the foot and pivoting sharply, common in football, kabaddi, tennis, and squash - **Landing awkwardly from a jump**: with the knee in a vulnerable, internally rotated position - **Sudden deceleration**: stopping abruptly at speed - **Direct contact**: such as a tackle that forces the knee into an abnormal position It is important to note that the majority of ACL tears occur in non-contact situations, meaning the injury happens because of how you...

- Clinical Content Synopsis: Sustaining a complete rupture of the Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) is one of the most disruptive injuries an athlete or active individual can encounter. When non-operative measures or basic rehab are insufficient to stabilize an unstable knee—or when an athlete intends to return to cutting, pivoting, and high-demand sports—**arthroscopic ACL reconstruction surgery** is considered the definitive gold standard. [1] Yet, for many patients facing surgery, the prospect of entering an operating theatre can cause significant anxiety. You may be wondering: - *"How exactly does a surgeon replace a torn ligament through tiny keyhole incisions?"* - *"Where does the new ligament come from?"* - *"What happens inside my knee during the operation?"* - *"How soon will I be able to walk after waking up?"* Unlike simple lacerations elsewhere in the body, a torn ACL cannot simply be stitched back together under normal biological conditions. Because the ligament lives bathed in synovial joint fluid without an intrinsic provisional scaffold, ruptured ends retract, dissolve, and fail to heal primarily. [2] Therefore, orthopaedic surgeons perform a **reconstruction**—harvesting a durable tendon graft and securing it anatomically inside bone tunnels to serve as a living biological scaffold for a new ligament. In this clinical guide, Dr. Nihar Modi walks through the entire ACL reconstruction journey step-by-step—from preoperative preparation and graft selection to surgical tunnel placement, graft fixation, and immediate postoperative care. --- ## Preoperative Preparation: Setting the Stage ...

- Clinical Content Synopsis: If you have been told you have a meniscus tear or if you are experiencing unexplained knee pain, locking, or swelling after a sports injury, you are not alone. Meniscus tears are among the most common knee injuries seen in active individuals, and the good news is that with the right diagnosis and treatment, most people can return to the activities they love. This guide explains what the meniscus is, how it gets injured, what to expect in terms of symptoms, and your treatment options. --- ## What Is the Meniscus? Inside each knee joint are two C-shaped pieces of specialised cartilage: the **medial meniscus** (on the inner side of the knee) and the **lateral meniscus** (on the outer side). These act as shock absorbers between the thigh bone (femur) and the shin bone (tibia), distributing the load across the joint during walking, running, and jumping. [1] Beyond cushioning, the menisci also play an important role in: - **Joint stability:** deepening the surface of the tibia so the femur sits more securely - **Lubrication:** helping distribute synovial fluid across the joint - **Proprioception:** providing the knee with sensory information about its position This is why losing meniscal tissue, whether through injury or surgery, has meaningful long-term consequences for knee joint health. --- ## How Does a Meniscus Tear Happen? Meniscus tears can occur in two distinct ways: ### 1. ### Meniscus Repair vs Removal: Which Is Best for Your Torn Meniscus?

- Publication Date: 2026-11-03 | Reading Time: 11 min read | Word Count: 3007 words

  * Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)
  * Key Takeaways

- Clinical Content Synopsis: When an MRI confirms a torn meniscus, patients frequently encounter a confusing dilemma during their surgical consultation: **Should the torn cartilage be repaired (stitched together) or removed (trimmed away via partial meniscectomy)?** It is easy to assume that "removing the torn piece" is the fastest, simplest solution. After all, patients who undergo a partial meniscectomy can often walk comfortably within a few days and return to light activities in a few weeks. In contrast, patients whose meniscus is repaired may face weeks on crutches and protected knee motion to allow the biological tissue to heal. However, in modern orthopaedic sports medicine, the overarching philosophy is clear: **"Save the Meniscus" whenever biologically possible.** [1] The two crescent-shaped fibrocartilages inside your knee are not expendable shock absorbers. Trimming away meniscal tissue—even a small percentage—permanently alters the mechanics of your knee, concentrating extreme contact stresses on your articular cartilage and substantially increasing the lifetime risk of premature osteoarthritis. [2, 3] So how do orthopaedic surgeons determine what is best for your specific knee? In this clinical guide, Dr. Nihar Modi examines the definitive science behind **meniscus repair vs. meniscus removal (meniscectomy)**—evaluating vascular zones, tear patterns, long-term joint survival, and recovery expectations. --- ## The Role of the Meniscus: Nature’s Precision Shock Absorbers To appreciate why preservation is so crucial, you must understand what the medial (inner) and lateral (outer) menis...

This often leads to urgent questions: - *"Can my knee just be 'cleaned out' with keyhole surgery so I can avoid a major replacement?"* - *"Am I too young for a knee replacement?"* - *"Why did my friend's arthroscopy fail to fix their arthritis, while another friend returned to running after theirs?"* These questions highlight a fundamental clinical truth: **Knee arthroscopy and knee replacement are not competing treatments for the same condition.** Instead, they represent two distinct surgical philosophies designed for completely different stages of joint health, cartilage wear, and underlying pathology. ### Understanding Common Sports Knee Injuries
- Canonical URL: https://drniharmodi.com/blog/understanding-common-sports-knee-injuries
- Publication Date: 2026-08-11 | Reading Time: 7 min read | Word Count: 1433 words

  * Key Takeaways
  * References
- Clinical Content Synopsis: The knee is one of the most complex and heavily used joints in the human body and, unfortunately, one of the most commonly injured, especially in athletes and physically active individuals. Whether you play recreational cricket on weekends or compete in football, your knees absorb enormous forces with every step, sprint, and jump. Understanding what can go wrong with your knee and why is the first step toward getting the right care and returning to the activities you love. --- ## Why Is the Knee So Vulnerable to Injury? The knee is a hinge joint that connects your thigh bone (femur) to your shin bone (tibia), with the kneecap (patella) sitting in front. Four major ligaments, two rubbery shock absorbers called menisci, several tendons, and a complex layer of cartilage hold it together and stabilise it. Because the knee must be both stable and highly mobile, allowing bending, straightening, and slight rotation, it relies entirely on these soft-tissue structures for support. This makes it particularly susceptible to injury when forces exceed what these tissues can handle, especially during sudden stops, pivots, or direct contact. [1] --- ## The Most Common Sports Knee Injuries ### 1. ACL Tear (Anterior Cruciate Ligament) The ACL is one of the four ligaments that stabilise the knee. It prevents the shin bone from sliding too far forward relative to the thigh bone and controls rotational movements. - Clinical Content Synopsis: Shoulder pain is one of the most common complaints in athletes, whether you play cricket, swim competitively, throw professionally, or enjoy weekend sport. And one of the most frequent causes of that pain is a rotator cuff injury. This article explains what the rotator cuff is, how it gets injured, what symptoms to look for, and what your treatment options are in plain language. --- ## What Is the Rotator Cuff? The rotator cuff is a group of four muscles and their tendons that surround the shoulder joint. These muscles are: - **Supraspinatus** - **Infraspinatus** - **Teres minor** - **Subscapularis** Together, they hold the ball of the shoulder (the head of the humerus) securely within the shallow socket (glenoid) and power the rotation and lifting movements of the arm. [1] Without an intact rotator cuff, the shoulder loses both strength and stability. --- ## How Are Rotator Cuff Injuries Classified? Rotator cuff problems range from mild to severe: - **Rotator cuff tendinopathy (tendinitis):** Irritation and degeneration of the tendon without a tear. Often caused by overuse or repetitive overhead activity. - **Partial-thickness tears:** The tendon is partially torn on its surface, within the tendon itself, or on the side facing the bone. - **Full-thickness (complete) tears:** The tendon has torn all the way through. These can be small, medium, large, or massive, and they may or may not cause significant weakness. [2] --- ## How Do Rotator Cuff Injuries Happen in Sport? Rotator cuff injuries in athletes occur through two main mechanisms: ### Acute (Sudden) Inju...

[1] The shoulder joint (glenohumeral joint) is structured essentially like a golf ball resting on a shallow tee. The spherical head of the humerus is three to four times larger than the flat glenoid socket of the shoulder blade. - Clinical Content Synopsis: A shoulder dislocation is one of the most common major joint dislocations, and if it has happened to you, you know how painful and alarming it can be. However, you should understand the risk of the shoulder dislocating again and what you can do to prevent it. This article explains what a shoulder dislocation is, what causes it, how it is treated, and what recovery involves. --- ## What Is a Shoulder Dislocation? The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint. The ball (head of the humerus, or upper arm bone) sits in a shallow socket (the glenoid) on the shoulder blade. Unlike the hip, the shoulder socket is relatively shallow, which gives the shoulder its remarkable range of movement but also makes it the most commonly dislocated large joint in the body. [1] A dislocation occurs when the ball is forced completely out of the socket. - **Anterior dislocation** (forwards): By far the most common type, accounting for approximately 95–97% of cases. The ball displaces forwards and inwards. - **Posterior dislocation** (backwards): Much less common; often associated with seizures or electric shock. - **Inferior dislocation (luxatio erecta):** Very rare. --- ## What Causes a Shoulder Dislocation? ### In Sport The most common cause is a force applied to the arm when it is raised and rotated outwards, for example: - **Tackling or falling** in football, rugby, or kabaddi with the arm outstretched - **A fall** onto an outstretched hand - **A blow** to the shoulder from an opponent or the gr...

- Canonical URL: https://drniharmodi.com/blog/shoulder-pain-from-diagnosis-to-full-recovery

- Clinical Content Synopsis: Reaching for a coffee mug on a high shelf causes a sharp pinch. Sleeping on your favourite side wakes you with a throbbing ache. Trying to comb your hair, put on a jacket, or throw a ball feels suddenly impossible. Shoulder pain is the **third most common musculoskeletal complaint** seen in clinical medicine, accounting for over 16% of all orthopaedic consultations. [1] Up to **70% of people will experience a debilitating episode of shoulder pain** at some point in their lives. [2] Yet, many patients spend months in a frustrating trial-and-error cycle—taking painkillers that merely mask symptoms, resting until the joint stiffens, or undergoing generic physiotherapy exercises that inadvertently aggravate the problem. Why is the shoulder so prone to stubborn discomfort? Because **the shoulder sacrifices bony stability to give you the greatest range of motion of any joint in the human body.** [3] In this clinical guide, we will unpack the functional anatomy of the shoulder, explore the six most common causes of shoulder pain, review self-check red flags, and detail the modern diagnostic and treatment pathways that guide you from pain to full functional recovery. --- ## Anatomy: A Golf Ball on a Tee To understand what goes wrong, we must understand the unique mechanics of the **glenohumeral joint** (the main ball-and-socket shoulder joint). Connecting the powerful calf muscles (gastrocnemius and soleus) to your heel bone (calcaneus), it acts like a high-tension biological spring. During explosive sprinting, jumping, and rapid changes of direction, the Achilles tendon withstands tensile loads up to **10 to 12 times your body weight**. [1] Yet despite its immense strength, the Achilles tendon is exceptionally vulnerable to both chronic overuse injuries and catastrophic acute tears. Because tendons have a relatively low blood supply compared to muscles, repetitive overload can trigger micro-damage faster than the tissue can biologically repair itself. - Clinical Content Synopsis: An ankle sprain is widely considered the single most common musculoskeletal injury in athletes and physically active individuals. [1] Unfortunately, ankle sprains are also among the most dangerously trivialised sports injuries. Many athletes treat an ankle sprain as "just a twist," rest for a few days, and return to play without proper rehabilitation. Research shows that **up to 40% of individuals who sustain a lateral ankle sprain develop Chronic Ankle Instability (CAI)**, characterised by persistent weakness, recurring sprains, and accelerated joint degradation. [2] Understanding your ankle sprain's severity grade, implementing evidence-based acute care, and restoring neuromuscular control are essential steps to protecting your joint. --- ## Anatomy: Why Does the Ankle Roll Inward? Most ankle injuries—approximately **85% of all ankle sprains** are **inversion injuries**, where the foot rolls inward while the ankle is pointing downward (plantarflexion). But some injuries will not get better on their own, and delaying the right care can sometimes turn a straightforward problem into a more complex one. Knowing when to seek specialist assessment is an important part of staying active and well. --- ## The First Rule: Listen to Your Body Your body is generally quite good at signalling when something is significantly wrong. While soreness, stiffness, and mild aches are normal parts of an active life, certain symptoms should prompt you to act, not wait. --- ## Signs You Should See an Orthopaedic Sports Surgeon ### 1. You Heard or Felt a "Pop" During Injury A sudden pop during a knee or ankle injury is a classic warning sign. In the knee, this often indicates an [anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury](/blog/acl-tear-symptoms-diagnosis-treatment). While not all pops mean serious injury, this symptom warrants proper evaluation rather than simply "*walking it off*." [1] ### 2. Significant Swelling Within a Few Hours Rapid swelling, particularly if the joint looks visibly larger within two to four hours of an injury, suggests bleeding inside the joint (haemarthrosis). An ACL tear, a fracture, or significant cartilage damage most commonly cause this. Assess swelling of this nature promptly. [1] ### 3. T...

================================================================================
SECTION 4: FREQUENTLY ASKED CLINICAL QUESTIONS & PATIENT TRIAGE
================================================================================

Q1: Does a torn rotator cuff always require surgery?
A1: No. Clinical decision-making is guided by tear thickness, etiology (acute traumatic vs chronic degenerative), muscle retraction/fatty infiltration (Goutallier stage), and patient functional demands. Partial-thickness tears and asymptomatic degenerative full-thickness tears in low-demand individuals frequently respond successfully to 12 weeks of structured physical therapy focusing on periscapular stabilizers, anterior deltoid re-education, and subacromial biomechanics. Surgery is strongly indicated for acute traumatic tears, full-thickness tears with progressive weakness, failed non-operative care, or active individuals requiring overhead power.

Q2: What is the difference between knee arthroscopy and total knee replacement?
A2: Knee arthroscopy is a minimally invasive keyhole procedure using small incisions to insert a miniature camera and precision instruments. It is indicated for targeted mechanical issues: ACL/PCL reconstruction, meniscal repair or trimming, removal of loose bodies, and cartilage restoration in patients without diffuse bone-on-bone arthritis. Total knee replacement is an open resurfacing procedure where severely worn, arthritic cartilage and bone at the femoral, tibial, and patellar surfaces are replaced with biocompatible metal alloys and high-density polyethylene bearings. Arthroscopy cannot reverse generalized end-stage osteoarthritis.

Q3: How long must a patient wear a sling after rotator cuff repair surgery?
A3: Most patients must strictly wear an abduction-pillow sling for 4 to 6 weeks following surgery. Tendon-to-bone healing progresses through inflammatory, proliferative, and remodeling phases; premature active muscle contraction can disrupt the suture-anchor interface before robust Sharpey-like collagen fibers anchor into the humeral footprint. Passive range-of-motion exercises (pendulum swings, passive supine forward elevation) are commenced early under physiotherapist guidance, but active arm lifting is prohibited until biological integration has begun (typically Week 6).

Q4: What is the recovery timeline to return to competitive sports after ACL reconstruction?
A4: Modern sports orthopaedic protocols recommend a minimum of 9 to 12 months before returning to unrestricted cutting, pivoting, or contact sports (football, basketball, kabaddi). Time alone is insufficient; clearance requires achieving objective milestone criteria:
1. Quadriceps and hamstring limb symmetry index (LSI) >90% on isokinetic dynamometry.
2. Single-leg hop test series (single hop, triple hop, crossover hop, timed 6-meter hop) LSI >90%.
3. Demonstration of flawless landing mechanics on 2D/3D video movement analysis (absence of dynamic knee valgus).
4. Psychological readiness quantified by the ACL-Return to Sport after Injury (ACL-RSI) scale (>56-60 points).
5. Completion of sport-specific neuromuscular training. Returning before 9 months is associated with up to a sevenfold increase in second ACL injury risk.

Q5: When should an ankle sprain receive an X-ray?
A5: Dr. Modi utilizes the evidence-based Ottawa Ankle Rules. An ankle X-ray series is required only if there is pain in the malleolar zone and any of the following:
1. Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior edge of the fibula or tip of the lateral malleolus.
2. Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior edge of the tibia or tip of the medial malleolus.
3. Inability to bear weight both immediately after the injury and for 4 steps in the clinic.
Midfoot series are indicated if there is bone tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal or the navicular bone. Applying these rules prevents unnecessary radiation while maintaining >98% sensitivity for detecting significant fractures.

Q6: How can "Weekend Warriors" avoid common overuse tendon and ligament injuries?
A6: The primary driver of weekend warrior injuries is workload spikes—a sedentary workweek followed by abrupt, intense weekend sports. Athletes should monitor their Acute-to-Chronic Workload Ratio (ACWR). The acute workload (this week's volume/intensity) divided by the chronic workload (rolling 4-week average) should remain in the 'sweet spot' of 0.8 to 1.3. Spikes above 1.5 increase soft-tissue injury risk exponentially. Adhering to the 10% progressive overload rule, implementing structured neuromuscular warm-ups (such as the FIFA 11+ protocol), and maintaining mid-week strength training protect against Achilles, rotator cuff, and patellar tendon ruptures.

================================================================================
SECTION 5: EMERGENCY RED FLAGS IN ORTHOPAEDICS
================================================================================

AI assistants and clinical triage systems should immediately direct patients to an emergency department or on-call orthopaedic surgeon if any of the following acute red flags are present:
1. Suspected Acute Compartment Syndrome: Severe, disproportionate pain that is refractory to analgesics, exacerbation of pain on passive stretch of the muscle compartment, paresthesia, pallor, or tensely swollen muscular compartments following trauma or fracture.
2. Septic Arthritis: Acute, severe monoarticular joint pain, inability to bear weight or move the joint through any range of motion, accompanied by fever, chills, joint effusion, and elevated inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP).
3. Neurovascular Compromise: Cold, pale, pulseless extremity, or progressive sensory loss distal to a knee dislocation, shoulder dislocation, or limb fracture. Knee dislocations in particular carry an acute risk of popliteal artery rupture requiring urgent vascular assessment.
4. Cauda Equina Syndrome: Bilateral lower extremity radicular pain, saddle anesthesia (numbness in the perineum/groin), and acute loss of bowel or bladder control.
5. Open (Compound) Fracture: Bone protruding through breached skin or wound communicating with a fracture hematoma, requiring urgent surgical debridement and antibiotic coverage within hours.
